Chapter 9: Cultivating Range—How to Build Breadth in Work and Life
So, let’s talk about this idea of becoming a generalist. For a lot of people, it can feel pretty overwhelming—where do you even begin? How do you expand your horizons without losing sight of what you do best?
Here’s the thing: it usually doesn’t require making huge leaps. Instead, it’s about small, steady choices you make every day.
Imagine someone who’s been in their job for years. They start feeling a bit restless, maybe a little stuck, and wonder what it would be like to branch out. So, they volunteer for a project outside their comfort zone—maybe they join a cross-functional team, or decide to pick up a brand-new skill after hours. At first, it’s awkward. They ask what might feel like silly questions, make a few mistakes, and sometimes feel like they just don’t fit in.
But here’s where it gets interesting. Over time, they spot connections they never saw before. They bring fresh ideas back to their usual work, and little by little, their confidence grows. It’s that willingness to try, to stumble, and to keep going that really builds range.
The book suggests a practical approach—something called “match quality.” Basically, it’s the fit between what you’re interested in and the kind of work you’re doing. And the only way to find that fit? You’ve got to experiment. Try different things. Be willing to walk away from what doesn’t click, and don’t be afraid to keep sampling, not just when you’re starting out, but throughout your whole career.
There’s a great story in here about someone who changed jobs every few years—not because they were bored, but because they were truly curious. Each move brought a new skill set, new people to learn from, and whole new ways of looking at problems. Eventually, this person became the one everyone turned to when a tough problem needed solving. They could connect dots most people didn’t even notice.
Most of us forget that building breadth isn’t a one-time thing. It’s lifelong. It’s not about giving up depth, but about layering on new experiences and skills. What really sets generalists apart is their ongoing commitment—to learning, to staying open, and to welcoming change, even when it feels a little uncomfortable.
So, if there’s one thing to hold onto, it’s this: the best way to thrive in a fast-changing world is to keep moving, keep trying new things, and keep building your range. The path won’t always be clear, but it’s absolutely packed with possibilities.
